<header class="hab-chapter-head"><span>VII</span><div><div class="hab-kicker">Vietnam · 12 subsections</div><h2 id="vietnam">Vietnam — Formation and transformations of Vietnamese Buddhist architecture</h2></div></header>

### 1. Three geographies for understanding Vietnamese Buddhist architecture {#vii-1}

Vietnamese Buddhist architecture does not follow a single evolutionary line. The North, Centre, and South were incorporated into different political, religious, and technical networks, and the monuments surviving today belong to different periods. It is also essential to distinguish the foundation date of a site from the date of its visible buildings: a very ancient monastery may have been rebuilt repeatedly and may preserve mainly seventeenth-, eighteenth-, or nineteenth-century architecture. The North contains the earliest centres around Luy Lâu and the Red River delta, followed by major royal foundations under the Lý <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">李朝</span>, the monastic landscapes of the Trần <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">陳朝</span>, and the large lowland compounds of the Restored Lê period. Central Vietnam developed a different relationship among monastery, dynasty, and landscape, especially at Huế. The South, meanwhile, brings together Vietnamese Mahāyāna chùa in Gia Định–Saigon and Khmer Theravāda traditions in the Mekong delta. Vietnamese diversity is therefore the product of several intersecting architectural histories rather than a single national style.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_1 alt="Three geographies for understanding Vietnamese Buddhist architecture" >}}

### 2. Luy Lâu and Chùa Dâu: from origins to architectural palimpsest {#vii-2}

The Luy Lâu <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">羸𨻻</span> region in present-day Bắc Ninh is one of the earliest centres of Buddhism in Vietnam. Chùa Dâu, associated with the cult of Pháp Vân and the Tứ Pháp <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">四法</span>, also demonstrates a fundamental problem in architectural history: the antiquity of a sacred place does not mean that its surviving buildings belong to its foundation period. Material traces of the earliest centuries have largely disappeared. The monastery was rebuilt on a major scale under the Trần, especially in the early fourteenth century, and was repeatedly transformed thereafter. Its present appearance largely reflects campaigns of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

Today the compound follows a nội công ngoại quốc <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">內工外國</span> type of organisation. The principal halls—tiền đường, thiêu hương, and thượng điện—form a hierarchical core enclosed by galleries and peripheral buildings. The Hòa Phong tower rises in the courtyard, a surviving portion of a formerly taller tower that introduces strong vertical emphasis into an otherwise horizontal complex. Chùa Dâu is therefore less an intact example of “second-century architecture” than a genuine palimpsest: a foundational site repeatedly rebuilt, where the memory of early Vietnamese Buddhism is carried by much later architecture.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_2 alt="Luy Lâu and Chùa Dâu: from origins to architectural palimpsest" >}}

### 3. The Lý and Chùa Phật Tích: the monumental royal monastery {#vii-3}

Under the Lý dynasty <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">李朝</span>, Buddhism became closely associated with the monarchy of Đại Việt <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">大越</span>. Chùa Phật Tích in Bắc Ninh is one of the most important sites for understanding this monumentalisation. Archaeological remains and stone sculpture reveal an exceptionally ambitious programme: terraces constructed on the hillside, a monumental stone Buddha, stone animals, and above all the foundations of a Lý-period tower whose scale and construction technique indicate a major building.

The relationship between monastery and mountain is crucial. Rather than occupying a regular plain, the complex unfolds in levels, using stairs, retaining walls, and platforms to turn the slope into an ascending ritual route. Excavations also indicate that the Lý-period layout differed markedly from later reconstructions, with the great tower playing a structuring role in the composition. Phật Tích is therefore exemplary for distinguishing the medieval archaeological monument from the reconstructed sanctuary visible today. More broadly, it shows that an eleventh-century Vietnamese royal monastery could combine architecture, monumental sculpture, and topography in an ambitious representation of Buddhist kingship.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_3 alt="The Lý and Chùa Phật Tích: the monumental royal monastery" >}}

### 4. Chùa Một Cột: symbolic pavilion and architecture of water {#vii-4}

Chùa Một Cột <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">一柱寺</span>, Hanoi’s One Pillar Pagoda, represents another Lý-period architectural experiment. Tradition attributes its foundation to King Lý Thái Tông <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">李太宗</span> in 1049. Unlike the expansive complex at Phật Tích, this monument condenses its meaning into a compact architectural image: a small timber pavilion raised above a pond to evoke a lotus emerging from the water.

The present structure is a reconstruction and should not be treated materially as the eleventh-century building. Its significance lies in the persistence of the spatial principle: pond, central support, and pavilion operate as a single composition. Symbolism is therefore not merely applied as decoration; it is produced by the structure itself. Chùa Một Cột reminds us that Lý Buddhist architecture was not limited to large axial monasteries. It could also take the form of a highly concentrated device in which water, structure, and iconography become inseparable.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_4 alt="Chùa Một Cột: symbolic pavilion and architecture of water" >}}

### 5. The Trần and Yên Tử: the mountain becomes a monastery {#vii-5}

Under the Trần dynasty <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">陳朝</span>, Yên Tử <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">安子</span> became the heartland of Trúc Lâm Buddhism <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">竹林</span>, especially associated with the king-monk Trần Nhân Tông. Yet Yên Tử cannot be understood as a single monastery. It is an extended religious landscape made up of pagodas, shrines, hermitages, funerary stupas, archaeological remains, and routes distributed across the mountain.

This dispersion turns movement itself into an architectural component. Pilgrims progress by stages, cross gates, reach terraces, follow ridges and valleys, and encounter successive ritual spaces. Buildings use topography rather than neutralising it: orientation, changes in altitude, and viewpoints contribute to religious hierarchy. Yên Tử therefore changes the scale of the architectural problem. The monastery is no longer only a cluster of buildings around a courtyard but a sacred territory structured through movement. The 2025 inscription of the Yên Tử–Vĩnh Nghiêm–Côn Sơn, Kiếp Bạc complex on the World Heritage List emphasises precisely this relationship among monuments, religious practice, and landscape.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_5 alt="The Trần and Yên Tử: the mountain becomes a monastery" >}}

### 6. Chùa Thầy: water, bridges, and the rebuilding of a medieval site {#vii-6}

Chùa Thầy, at the foot of Sài Sơn near Hanoi, was founded in the Lý period and is closely associated with the master Từ Đạo Hạnh. Architecturally, however, its importance also lies in the extensive transformations carried out over later centuries, particularly under the Mạc and during the seventeenth century. Like Chùa Dâu, it is a palimpsest through which a medieval sacred place survives in later architecture.

The principal composition faces Long Trì Lake. The Thủy Đình, a pavilion set in the water beneath an eight-roof composition, originally served a symbolic function and later became the celebrated stage for water puppetry. The covered Nhật Tiên and Nguyệt Tiên bridges, built in the early seventeenth century, connect banks and small islands. Behind this watery foreground stand the principal halls and galleries, while paths continue toward the mountain, caves, and secondary sanctuaries. Chùa Thầy is therefore crucial for understanding how a Vietnamese monastery may be composed through buildings, bridges, water, and relief rather than through a single axial sequence of halls.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_6 alt="Chùa Thầy: water, bridges, and the rebuilding of a medieval site" >}}

### 7. The Restored Lê and Chùa Bút Tháp: the great lowland monastery {#vii-7}

Chùa Bút Tháp, or Ninh Phúc tự, is one of the best sites for understanding the mature form of the great monastery of the Red River delta. The site is older, but its present organisation derives primarily from the major seventeenth-century rebuilding under the Restored Lê. In contrast with mountain monasteries, Bút Tháp is a lowland compound whose hierarchy is generated through sequences of halls and courtyards.

The monastery follows a nội công ngoại quốc <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">內工外國</span> organisation. From the entrance, the tam quan, bell tower, tiền đường, thiêu hương, and thượng điện succeed one another, while galleries and lateral buildings surround the ritual core. The deeper one moves into the complex, the denser the image programme and the more restricted the sacred space. Báo Nghiêm tower introduces a vertical and funerary element into this horizontal composition. Bút Tháp also integrates architecture with timber and stone sculpture and major image programmes, including the celebrated thousand-armed, thousand-eyed Avalokiteśvara. It offers an essential counterpoint to Yên Tử: here it is not the mountain but the geometry of courts, galleries, and halls that organises the monastery.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_7 alt="The Restored Lê and Chùa Bút Tháp: the great lowland monastery" >}}

### 8. Chùa Hương: from monastery to pilgrimage territory {#vii-8}

The Hương Sơn complex, commonly called Chùa Hương, takes the integration of landscape and religious experience even further. It is not a single pagoda but a broad network of sanctuaries, temples, caves, and pilgrimage stages distributed through a karst landscape southwest of Hanoi. Several routes connect its component sites; travel by river and ascent toward the sanctuaries are integral parts of the ritual system.

Thiên Trù forms an important built centre of courtyards and halls, but the route continues toward Hương Tích Cave. There the natural cavity itself becomes the sanctuary: architecture no longer encloses sacred space in a building but organises access to a mountain understood as a threshold to another religious realm. Chùa Hương therefore dissolves the simple opposition between architecture and nature. Stairs, landing places, paths, gates, caves, and pavilions together form an infrastructure of pilgrimage. The monument is less a single building than a territory placed into ritual sequence.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_8 alt="Chùa Hương: from monastery to pilgrimage territory" >}}

### 9. What northern monasteries reveal: plans, timber, towers, and landscapes {#vii-9}

The major northern sites demonstrate that there is no single Vietnamese monastery plan. Chùa Dâu and Bút Tháp show the depth of lowland compounds, successive courts, and nội công ngoại quốc <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">內工外國</span> arrangements. Phật Tích turns a slope into monumental terraces. Yên Tử and Hương Sơn make movement through mountains part of architecture itself. Chùa Thầy instead establishes a triangular relationship among halls, water, and relief.

Despite these differences, several principles recur. Timber framing forms the structural skeleton of many halls, while walls generally enclose rather than carry the building. Large roofs protect against heavy rainfall and create broad zones of shade. Towers, tháp <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">塔</span>, may serve reliquary, funerary, or monumental functions and introduce vertical accents into complexes dominated by horizontal rooflines. Finally, the material history of each site demands a stratigraphic reading: foundations, sculptures, frames, and visible plans may belong to different campaigns. Vietnamese Buddhist architecture must therefore be read as a sequence of transformations rather than the static survival of an ancient prototype.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_9 alt="What northern monasteries reveal: plans, timber, towers, and landscapes" >}}

### 10. Central Vietnam: Huế and Chùa Thiên Mụ {#vii-10}

In central Vietnam, Huế developed a distinctive relationship among Buddhism, the Nguyễn dynasty <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">阮朝</span>, and the river landscape. Chùa Thiên Mụ <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">天姥寺</span>, set on a height above the Perfume River, Hương Giang <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">香江</span>, is the defining example. Tradition places its foundation in the early seventeenth century under the Nguyễn lords, before Huế became the imperial capital.

In the nineteenth century the complex received major monumental investment. Between 1844 and 1846 Emperor Thiệu Trị <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">紹治帝</span> commissioned Phước Duyên tower <span class="hab-han" lang="vi">福緣塔</span>, a seven-storeyed structure near the entrance. Visible from the river, it functions as a territorial marker as well as a religious monument. Behind it, gates, courtyards, halls, and monastic spaces unfold in sequence. Thiên Mụ therefore differs from the great lowland compounds of the North: its identity depends strongly on the relationship among promontory, river, entrance axis, and signal tower. Architecture here participates in constructing the political landscape of the Nguyễn capital.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_10 alt="Central Vietnam: Huế and Chùa Thiên Mụ" >}}

### 11. The South: Gia Định–Saigon and the Mekong Delta {#vii-11}

In southern Vietnam, the history of Mahāyāna Buddhist architecture followed a distinct trajectory linked to the formation of Gia Định, the growth of Saigon, and the expansion of monastic networks across Nam Bộ. Southern monasteries did not merely reproduce northern forms: traditional layouts were adapted to local materials, ritual needs, and increasingly urban or deltaic settings.

Chùa Giác Lâm, founded in 1744 on Cẩm Sơn Mound, is the major early reference point. It became an ancestral monastery of the Lâm Tế lineage and an important centre of monastic training. Its tam-character (三) layout is organised around the chánh điện, giảng đường, and nhà trai. Timber framing, massive columns, carved cửa võng screens, and dense image programmes give the sanctuary its characteristic depth. In front of the main complex, the seven-storeyed hexagonal Bửu tháp Xá Lợi now introduces a strong vertical element into a monastery historically dominated by horizontal rooflines. The many funerary towers in the grounds also underline the lineage function of the institution.

Chùa Giác Viên, which developed from a sanctuary connected with Giác Lâm and was reshaped in the nineteenth century, extends this tradition. Its timber construction, âm dương tiles, and carvings of plants and fruits associated with Nam Bộ show how the older chùa vocabulary became rooted in a specifically southern visual culture.

In the Mekong Delta, Chùa Vĩnh Tràng at Mỹ Tho is another essential landmark. Developed in the nineteenth century and completed as a major monastery in 1849, it enlarges principles already visible at Giác Lâm: five building ranges, two light courts, and a very large number of columns structure an extensive Mahāyāna compound. Its decoration combines Vietnamese and Chinese forms with European elements, making it one of the clearest examples of southern architectural eclecticism in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

Twentieth-century Saigon then produced new forms of urban Buddhist monumentality. Chùa Xá Lợi, built between 1956 and 1958, places its principal sanctuary on the upper floor and clearly separates the seven-storeyed bell tower from the main worship building. Chùa Vĩnh Nghiêm, begun in 1964 and completed in 1971, translates a vocabulary inspired by major northern monasteries into the southern metropolis: a chữ công plan, a two-level central building, a large Buddha hall with layered roofs, and a seven-storeyed Quán Thế Âm tower. Together these monuments show that southern Mahāyāna Buddhism was not limited to preserving the old monasteries of Gia Định; it also generated modern, monumental architecture adapted to the city.

Southern Mahāyāna architecture therefore forms a continuous but highly varied history: from the timber monasteries of Giác Lâm and Giác Viên to the eclecticism of Vĩnh Tràng and the large urban complexes of Xá Lợi and Vĩnh Nghiêm, architectural forms changed substantially while retaining the central role of the Buddha hall, teaching spaces, and vertical monuments.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_11 alt="The South: Gia Định–Saigon and the Mekong Delta" >}}

### 12. An architecture of accumulation: images, altars, and memories {#vii-12}

Across these regional differences, many Vietnamese monasteries share a strong capacity for accumulation. Sanctuaries may bring together Buddhas, bodhisattvas, arhats, lineage masters, guardians, local deities, and ancestor-related cults. This plurality does not imply a lack of order: images are hierarchised through position, height, and the depth of the halls.

Architecture makes such layering possible. A new cult may be accommodated through an additional altar, lateral hall, or pavilion without necessarily erasing earlier layers. The same principle applies to the buildings themselves: a Lý-period site may preserve a Lê-period timber frame, a Nguyễn tower, and contemporary restorations while continuing to carry a medieval memory. The Vietnamese monastery is therefore less a fixed object than a historical organism. Understanding its architecture requires identifying the different layers—plan, structure, decoration, images, landscape, and uses—that accumulated over time.

{{< hab-image illustrations.part_vii.section_12 alt="An architecture of accumulation: images, altars, and memories" >}}
